rationale: Mixed-methods primary study of WASH challenges on Chilwa Island, Zambia. Although it touches on household/community water access and sanitation infrastructure (C1, C4) using empirical survey and interview data (C3), its explicit exposure scope is socio-economic, cultural, and environmental factors shaping WASH practices rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, tenure, tariff, or institutional mechanism governing service access (fails C2; exclude under E03).
plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence between plain and narrow Criterion 2 readings: the study focuses exclusively on socio-economic, cultural, and environmental determinants of household WASH practices and infrastructure scarcity in a remote settlement, without examining any legal, administrative, regulatory, institutional, or governance mechanism.

evidence_quotes.quote: The main goal shall be to assess socio-economic, cultural, and environmental factors influencing compliance with WASH and to recommend suitable evidence-based interventions to improve health outcomes.

Analysis of this data highlights insufficient access to clean water, deeply held cultural beliefs that guide hygiene practices, and grossly inadequate sanitation infrastructure as key barriers to effective WASH practices.
Using a mixed-methods approach, data were collected using structured surveys and in-depth interviews with residents, community leaders, and key informants.
